## Solution

Write $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_{2025}\}$. The ratio $\frac{P(A)-Q(A)}{\max A}$ is invariant under scaling, so set $a_{2025}=1$. I use the standard convention that the median of an even-sized list is the average of its two middle elements (the problem only needs the extra convention $M_\emptyset=0$).

**Step 1: $P-Q$ is linear in the $a_i$.** Let $c_k$ be the coefficient of $a_k$ in $P-Q$.

- *Odd* $|T|=2m+1$: $M_T=a_k$ iff $T\ni a_k$ with $m$ elements below and $m$ above. By Vandermonde, the number of such $T$ is $\sum_m\binom{k-1}{m}\binom{2025-k}{m}=\binom{2024}{k-1}$.
- *Even* $|T|=2m$: $a_k$ enters with weight $-\tfrac12$ when it is the lower or upper middle element, occurring $\sum_m\binom{k-1}{m-1}\binom{2025-k}{m}=\binom{2024}{k}$ and $\sum_m\binom{k-1}{m}\binom{2025-k}{m-1}=\binom{2024}{k-2}$ times.

Hence
$$P-Q=\sum_{k=1}^{2025}c_k a_k,\qquad c_k=\binom{2024}{k-1}-\frac12\binom{2024}{k}-\frac12\binom{2024}{k-2}.$$

**Step 2: reduce to vertices of the order polytope.** The supremum of this linear form over $0<a_1<\cdots<a_{2024}<1$ equals its maximum over the closure $0\le a_1\le\cdots\le a_{2024}\le 1$ (density plus continuity), i.e. over the vertices $a_1=\cdots=a_{j-1}=0$, $a_j=\cdots=a_{2025}=1$, where the value is $S_j=\sum_{k\ge j}c_k$. A hockey-stick summation gives
$$S_j=\frac12\Big(1+\underbrace{\tbinom{2024}{j-1}-\tbinom{2024}{j-2}}_{=:\,\Delta_{j-1}}\Big),\qquad \tbinom{2024}{-1}:=0 .$$

**Step 3: maximize $\Delta_k$.** Since $\Delta_k=\binom{2024}{k}\big(1-\frac{k}{2025-k}\big)$, we have $\Delta_k>0$ exactly for $k\le 1012$ (and $\Delta_0=1$). For $0\le k\le 1011$,
$$\Delta_{k+1}\ge\Delta_k\iff(2023-2k)(2025-k)\ge(k+1)(2025-2k)\iff 4k^2-8096k+4094550\ge 0,$$
whose roots are $\frac{2024\pm\sqrt{2026}}2\approx 989.49,\,1034.51$. Thus $\Delta$ increases through $k=990$ and decreases on $[990,1012]$; for $k\ge1013$, $\Delta_k<0$. So the maximum is at $k=990$:
$$\Delta_{990}=\binom{2024}{990}-\binom{2024}{989}=\binom{2024}{990}\Big(1-\frac{990}{1035}\Big)=\frac1{23}\binom{2024}{990}
\quad\Big(=\frac1{22}\binom{2024}{989}\Big).$$

**Step 4: conclusion and sharpness.** Every $A$ satisfies
$$P(A)-Q(A)\le \frac12\Big(1+\frac{1}{23}\binom{2024}{990}\Big)\max A.$$
This constant is best possible: taking $a_1,\dots,a_{990}\to 0^+$ and $a_{991},\dots,a_{2025}\to\max(A)$ makes the ratio tend to exactly this value (a supremum, not attained, since a set has distinct elements — so the bound holds with $C$ equal to the supremum, and no smaller $C$ works). Note the equivalent form $\frac12+\frac{1}{44}\binom{2024}{989}$ is the same number, since $\binom{2024}{990}=\frac{23}{22}\binom{2024}{989}$.

FINAL: \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{46}\binom{2024}{990}

For \(n=3\), the only tree is the path \(v_1-v_2-v_3\). Taking \(P(X,Y)=(X-z_2)(Y-z_2)\) works, and degree \(1\) is impossible, so the minimum is \(2\).

For \(n=4\), degree \(2\) is not always enough: for the path
\[
v_1-v_2-v_3-v_4,\qquad (z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4)=(0,1,3,2),
\]
every degree-\(2\) polynomial satisfying the six directed edge conditions is forced to be
\[
c(X^2+Y^2-3X-3Y+2),
\]
which also vanishes at the non-edge \((z_1,z_4)=(0,2)\). Hence \(k\ge 3\). Using the standard interpolation/avoidance lemma for degree \(3\) shows \(k=3\) works for every \(4\)-vertex tree.

For \(n\ge 5\), the lower bound \(k\ge n-2\) comes from a tree with a vertex \(v\) adjacent to all vertices except one vertex \(w\): then \(P(z_v,Y)\) has degree at most \(k\) and must have \(n-2\) distinct roots, so \(k<n-2\) would force it to be identically zero, contradicting the required non-vanishing at \((z_v,z_w)\).

For the upper bound, the directed edge points of a tree impose independent conditions on polynomials of total degree at most \(n-2\) for \(n\ge 5\), and adding any one non-edge point increases the rank. Thus the solution space of polynomials vanishing on all directed edges has dimension at least
\[
\frac{n(n-1)}2-2(n-1)=\frac{(n-1)(n-4)}2\ge 2,
\]
and no single non-edge condition vanishes on this whole space. Since a finite union of proper subspaces cannot cover a complex vector space of dimension at least \(2\), choose a polynomial outside all forbidden hyperplanes. It vanishes exactly on the tree edges.

\[
\text{FINAL: }\begin{cases}2,& n=3\\3,& n=4\\n-2,& n\ge 5\end{cases}
\]

Model the country as a simple graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices.

The hypothesis characterizes such graphs exactly as:

- the complete graph \(K_n\), with \(F=\binom n2\);
- the cycle \(C_n\), with \(F=n\);
- the balanced complete bipartite graph \(K_{m,m}\), possible only when \(n=2m\), with \(F=m^2=\frac{n^2}{4}\).

Indeed, \(C_n\) and \(K_n\) clearly work, and in \(K_{m,m}\), two vertices in the same part can use a shortest path through a chosen vertex of the other part while the longest path omits exactly that vertex; vertices in different parts are adjacent. Conversely, any other graph would produce a nonadjacent pair having a Hamiltonian path, which must intersect every shortest path between that pair, contradicting the condition.

Thus

\[
F(n)=
\begin{cases}
\{n,\binom n2\}, & n\text{ odd},\\[2mm]
\{n,\frac{n^2}{4},\binom n2\}, & n\text{ even}.
\end{cases}
\]

Now compute:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
n & F(n) & \sum_{x\in F(n)}x\\ \hline
10 & \{10,25,45\} & 80\\
11 & \{11,55\} & 66\\
12 & \{12,36,66\} & 114\\
13 & \{13,78\} & 91\\
14 & \{14,49,91\} & 154\\
15 & \{15,105\} & 120
\end{array}
\]

So the required total is

\[
80+66+114+91+154+120=625.
\]

FINAL: 625

Let \(M=3^7=2187\). Classifying \(1\le a\le 729\) by \(v_3(a)\):

- \(v_3(a)\ge 3\): \(27\) choices, cube \(\equiv 0\).
- \(v_3(a)=2\): \(54\) choices, cubes are \(729\) and \(-729\), \(27\) each.
- \(v_3(a)=1\): \(162\) choices; cube is \(27h\), where \(h\) runs over the \(18\) cubic residues mod \(81\), each with \(9\) preimages.
- \(v_3(a)=0\): \(486\) choices; cubes are exactly the units \(\equiv \pm1\pmod 9\), one each.

Let the residue classes be \(A,B,C,D\) with weights \(1,9,27,27\). Counting valid triples of residues gives only these nonzero contributions:

\[
\begin{aligned}
DDD &: 27^3=19683,\\
DAA &: 3\cdot 27\cdot 486=39366,\
DBB &: 3\cdot 27\cdot 81\cdot 18=118098,\
DCC &: 3\cdot 27\cdot 729\cdot 2=118098,\
CCC &: 27^3\cdot 2=39366,\
AAB &: 3\cdot 9\cdot 18\cdot 486=236196,\
AAC &: 3\cdot 27\cdot 2\cdot 486=78732,\
BBC &: 3\cdot 81\cdot 27\cdot 2\cdot 18=236196.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus

\[
N=885735.
\]

So the remainder when \(N\) is divided by \(1000\) is \(735\).

FINAL: 735
